name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,814

clue.text: Italian butterflies passenger catches drop dead

indicators.note: To catch something is to take hold of it, so the passenger's word closes around the other piece.

blocks.note: a fare is a paying passenger in a taxi
to fall is to die, as soldiers fall in battle

explanation.surface: Some Italian butterflies are so startling that a passenger is caught out by them.
explanation.walkthrough: Farfalle is the bow-shaped pasta; the Italian word literally means butterflies, so the definition is a translation as much as a description.
explanation.definitionFit: Farfalle is Italian for butterflies, the name given to the bow-tie pasta shape.

clue.text: Fitting a large person in the front row, so getting up

indicators.note: In a down clue, getting up means the letters climb the column, so they read from bottom to top.

blocks.note: used as it stands

blocks.clueFragment: large person in the front row
blocks.note: in rugby, the props are the heavy forwards at either end of the front row of the scrum
used as it stands, then turned round to OS

explanation.surface: A big person has been seated in the front row, which somebody finds fitting.
explanation.walkthrough: The front row here is the rugby scrum, not a theatre seat; a prop is one of the bulky forwards who pack down there.
explanation.definitionFit: Apropos means fitting or appropriate to the occasion.

clue.text: Dividing piece of fish, allow fighter no steak

indicators.note: Something dividing an object sits in the middle of it, splitting it in two.

blocks.note: a fin is part of a fish
to let is to allow
a MiG is a Russian fighter jet
used as it stands

explanation.surface: An order to split a piece of fish and deny a fighter his steak.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the very end; 'piece of fish' looks like the answer's meaning but only supplies the outer FIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Filet mignon is a tender steak cut from the small end of the beef tenderloin.

clue.text: Reveal unqualified lawyers bet on losing case

indicators.note: A case is the outer casing; losing it strips a word's first and last letters.

blocks.note: a lay person has no professional qualification
the Bar is the body of barristers
BET without its outer letters leaves E

explanation.surface: Exposing unqualified lawyers who put money on a case they are losing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' only places the E after BAR; 'losing case' works on 'bet', not on anything in court.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay bare is to reveal or expose something fully.

clue.text: Remove surplus empty chest

indicators.note: Emptying a word takes out its middle, leaving only the first and last letters.

blocks.note: surplus is extra
CHEST with its insides removed

explanation.surface: Clearing out a spare chest that has nothing in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'empty chest' as a noun phrase to throw out; in the wordplay, empty is an instruction applied to the word CHEST.
explanation.definitionFit: To extract something is to remove it, as a dentist extracts a tooth.

clue.text: Function on back street expected award for successful party

indicators.note: Going back means reading from right to left.

blocks.note: cos is short for cosine, a trigonometric function
St is the abbreviation for street, turned round to TS

explanation.surface: A back-street function where a successful party collects its expected prize.
explanation.walkthrough: The party is one side in a lawsuit, not a celebration: the winner of a court case is usually awarded its legal costs.
explanation.definitionFit: In court the successful party normally expects an award of costs against the loser.

clue.text: A vessel for storing and one for piping oil?

blocks.note: a can is a container for keeping food or drink
a vas is an anatomical duct, a vessel carrying fluid through the body

explanation.surface: A riddle about two kinds of vessel, one for storage and one for piping oil along.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes oil the thing being piped; it is really the definition, an oil painting, and the question mark flags that a canvas is only one example.
explanation.definitionFit: An oil painting is often called a canvas, after the cloth it is painted on.

clue.text: Icarus, finally ready to have feathers attached, played the hero

indicators.note: Finally points to the last letter of the word before it.

blocks.note: the last letter of Icarus
tar goes on first so the feathers stick, as in tarring and feathering

explanation.surface: Icarus, wings about to be fixed on, as the hero of his own legend.
explanation.walkthrough: Icarus flew on wings of feathers and wax, so the surface steers toward him; the feathers really belong to the old punishment of tarring and feathering.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor who starred played the lead, the hero of the piece.

clue.text: Team sounded disappointed without speaking in interview

indicators.note: An interview is spoken, so the word is heard rather than read.

blocks.note: a sigh is a wordless sound of disappointment

explanation.surface: A team in a post-match interview, letting out a disappointed noise instead of answering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without speaking' is part of the meaning: a sigh expresses disappointment with no words.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a sports team is called a side, one of the two sides of the contest.

clue.text: Maiden using her mouth in a virtuous way

blocks.note: m for maiden over is a cricket scoring abbreviation
orally means by mouth

explanation.surface: A maiden speaking up in a virtuous manner.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden in cricket is an over with no runs scored, written M on the scorecard.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: morals are principles of right conduct, so behaving by them is behaving virtuously.

clue.text: Noisy high speed's the usual way to show virility

blocks.note: Mach 1 is the speed of sound, so a speed measured in Mach is tied to noise
's is short for is
MO is modus operandi, one's usual way of working

explanation.surface: Roaring about at high speed as the standard way to prove you are a man.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mach number measures speed against the speed of sound, which is why 'noisy' joins 'high speed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Machismo is an exaggerated display of manly virility.

clue.text: Brown most of duck, turning that in pot

indicators.note: Most of a word is all but its last letter.
Turning a word round makes it read backwards.

blocks.note: tan is a light brown
DRAKE, a male duck, without its last letter, then turned round to KARD

explanation.surface: Browning most of a duck and turning it over in a cooking pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That' refers back to the shortened duck; the pot at the end is a drinking pot, not a cooking one.
explanation.definitionFit: A tankard is a pot, a large mug for beer.

clue.text: What was the point of Nelson's greatest triumph?

definitions.text: What was the point of Nelson's greatest triumph?

blocks.note: the surface asks what purpose the victory served; the setter means point as a headland, a cape jutting into the sea
Nelson's greatest victory was the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805, named after the nearby cape

explanation.surface: A question asking what Nelson's great victory was ultimately for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' reads as purpose; it is a point of land, the headland off which the Battle of Trafalgar was fought in 1805.
explanation.definitionFit: Cape Trafalgar is the headland on Spain's south-west coast that gave its name to Nelson's victory.

clue.text: Object of worship serious sorcerer keeps nuts in

indicators.note: Keeping something is holding it inside.
Nuts means crazy, so the letters of the word before it are scrambled.

blocks.note: grave means serious
IN scrambled
a mage is a magician

explanation.surface: A solemn wizard who hoards nuts as a sacred object.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' is not a thing kept but the instruction to scramble 'in'; GRAVE and MAGE together make the holder.
explanation.definitionFit: A graven image is a carved idol, an object of worship forbidden in the Ten Commandments.

clue.text: Men alone played a soulful song

indicators.note: Letters that are played are performed in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: the letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A group of men with nobody else playing a soul song.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram fits the surface: a song about leaning on someone, made from men who are alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Lean on Me is Bill Withers' 1972 soul song.

clue.text: Spark from burning church tower

blocks.note: a fire that is in is still burning
a spire is the pointed top of a church tower

explanation.surface: A spark flying off a church tower that is on fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spark' is a verb here, as in sparking an idea, though the surface makes it a fleck of fire.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative sense: inspiring an idea or movement sets it going, the way a spark starts a fire.

clue.text: Couple with no last make rotten cobblers

indicators.note: The word loses its last letter.

blocks.note: TWO, a couple, without its last letter
an addled egg has gone rotten

explanation.surface: A pair of shoemakers who have done shoddy work.
explanation.walkthrough: Cobblers is British slang for nonsense, not shoemakers; the rotten cobblers of the surface are really rubbish talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Twaddle and cobblers both mean nonsense.

clue.text: Show rug I want shortened

indicators.note: A shortened word loses its last letter.

blocks.note: a mat is a small rug
used as it stands
NEED, to want, without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone showing a rug they want cut down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' is the noun, a performance, rather than the verb the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: A matinee is an afternoon show at a theatre or cinema.

clue.text: Rum butler drinks marks glass

indicators.note: Rum means odd or strange, so the next word's letters come out oddly arranged.
What you drink goes inside you, so one piece takes in the other.

blocks.note: the letters of BUTLER scrambled
M is the abbreviation for mark, the old German currency, so marks gives M

explanation.surface: A peculiar butler who drinks until he leaves marks on the glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink the butler takes; it is the scramble signal, and the drink is left to 'drinks'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumbler is a flat-bottomed drinking glass.

clue.text: Passage right through bar

indicators.note: Passing through something puts one piece inside the other.

blocks.note: bar as in 'all bar one' means except
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A right of way running through a bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' is the preposition meaning except, not a pub or a rod.
explanation.definitionFit: An excerpt is a passage taken from a longer text or piece of music.

clue.text: Fed outside shelter, an old minstrel

indicators.note: One piece goes outside the other, wrapping round it.

blocks.note: a G-man, or Fed, is an FBI agent
the lee is the sheltered side, away from the wind

explanation.surface: A federal agent standing outside a shelter beside an old minstrel.
explanation.walkthrough: Fed is American slang for a federal agent, not the past tense of feed.
explanation.definitionFit: A gleeman was a medieval minstrel or singer of glees.

clue.text: New pain after switching silver filling

indicators.note: After places one piece following another.
Switching the two letters swaps their order.

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver, its letters switched
N is the abbreviation for new
an ache is a pain

explanation.surface: A fresh pain after a silver tooth filling has been changed.
explanation.walkthrough: The dental picture is a decoy: the filling is a chocolate cream for cakes and truffles.
explanation.definitionFit: Ganache is a chocolate and cream mixture used as a filling or icing.

clue.text: Cycling jersey to post, eBay item perhaps

blocks.note: to mail is to post
a lot is an item for sale at auction, of which an eBay listing is one example

explanation.surface: A cycling jersey someone has sold on eBay and needs to post.
explanation.walkthrough: The maillot jaune is the Tour de France leader's yellow jersey; 'perhaps' marks eBay as just one kind of auction.
explanation.definitionFit: A borrowing from French cycling, where the race leader wears the maillot jaune, the yellow jersey.

clue.text: Fresh coin not dim, in this initially?

definitions.text: Fresh coin not dim, in this initially?

indicators.note: Fresh means new, so the letters come out in a new order.
Initially takes the first letter of the word before it.

blocks.note: letters used as they stand, to be scrambled
the first letter of this

explanation.surface: A question: is a shiny new coin, not dulled, in this state from the start?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a fresh, bright coin is exactly one in mint condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue asks what state a fresh, undulled coin is in: the pristine state it had when newly struck.

clue.text: Valves when turned sprayed droplets

indicators.note: Turning a word round makes it read backwards.

blocks.note: taps are valves controlling the flow of water

explanation.surface: Taps that sprayed water when someone turned them on.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures turning a tap on; the turning is really done to the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Spat, from spit, means sent out droplets from the mouth.

clue.text: Discussion yearly with former champion at Wimbledon

blocks.note: p.a. is per annum, yearly
Rod Laver, the Australian who won Wimbledon four times

explanation.surface: An annual chat with a past Wimbledon winner.
explanation.walkthrough: Wimbledon is the London tennis championship; Rod Laver won it in the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: A palaver is a lengthy discussion, originally a parley between traders and local people.

clue.text: See 6
Bucket boy got from cleaning lady by dishonesty

blocks.note: a char, or charlady, is a British word for a cleaner
a lie is a piece of dishonesty

explanation.surface: A cleaner's bucket that a boy got hold of by cheating.
explanation.walkthrough: Bucket is a surname: Charlie Bucket is the boy hero of Roald Dahl's Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlie Bucket is the boy who wins the golden ticket in Roald Dahl's story.

clue.text: Thinner version of Proust in which nothing is forgotten

indicators.note: A new version rearranges the original.
Nothing is O, and forgetting it drops that letter.

blocks.note: PROUST with the O taken out, to be scrambled

explanation.surface: A slimmed-down edition of Proust, the author of In Search of Lost Time, in which nothing gets left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that Proust wrote the great novel of memory; here nothing, O, is literally forgotten. Turps is British short for turpentine.
explanation.definitionFit: Turps, short for turpentine, is a paint thinner.

clue.text: Modern stretches to 14C in the art world

indicators.note: RECENT stretches the word TO apart, sitting between its letters.

blocks.note: used as it stands
recent means modern

explanation.surface: Modern art reaching back as far as the fourteenth century.
explanation.walkthrough: 14C means the fourteenth century; 'to' reads as a link word but supplies the outer T and O.
explanation.definitionFit: Trecento is the Italian name for the 1300s, the 14th century, in art history.
